What a crisis is

Economics gives each civilization an economy that can go wrong: the world's business cycle, the loans it carries, the prices it trades at, the inflation idle Gold suffers. A crisis is the moment one of those readings crosses a line. It isn't rolled and it isn't saved for the end of the age; the mod reads the state of your economy every turn, and a crisis can start on any turn of any age. While it lasts, the World tab shows what's pulling you down and what you can do about it.

Each response you take changes something at once, costs you something, and leaves a legacy you carry for a while or for the rest of the age. The history is the guide: the choices Solon, Philip II, Isaac Newton and Franklin Roosevelt made are the choices on the panel, with their prices and their aftermath.
The six kinds

A Depression comes when your own index on the World tab falls under 0.80. A credit panic comes in Exploration (from the Banking stage) and Modern when a Panic freezes the lenders while you hold loans, or when a bubble bursts. A price shock comes when the price of a resource class you import or export has moved 40 percent, up or down, on ten turns ago. A debt crisis comes after three turns with your payments due above your income, or when you default on a loan from another civilization. Runaway inflation, once you have Public debt, comes after five turns with the rate at its cap (with the Inflation option on), or ten turns after you leave the gold standard. A trade collapse comes in Exploration and Modern when a third of your trade routes end within five turns.

A civilization has at most one crisis of a kind every 30 turns and two crises at once. A crisis ends the turn its condition stops holding, and the notice names what ended it: the responses you took, or the world recovering on its own.
The Crisis section

While a crisis is open, the World tab of the Economics screen opens a Crisis section above the index. It names the crisis, the turn it began and the events behind it; it lists the responses standing and how long each has left; and it offers the responses open to you this age, each with what it does now, what it costs and what it leaves. A response goes through at the start of the next turn, like a loan request. You can end a standing response early from the same section, and some remember being cut short.
Doing nothing, and the Hoover trap

Doing nothing is a choice too. The world's index drifts back toward 1.00 by a tenth of the gap each turn, so a Depression left alone lifts in time, unless the cycle's momentum and new bad news hold it down. Meanwhile the slump charge takes a share of your income, the bond market's rates rise with the gap, and a Panic freezes the lenders: all of it leaning the wrong way, as it did in 1930.

Two responses make it worse, as they did then. Raising tariffs in a Depression (Smoot-Hawley's line) has the computer players answer in kind, and once three civilizations hold a High tariff while the world is under 0.80 the trade war pulls the index down by 0.005 a turn on its own. Austerity (Andrew Mellon's line) repays debt and mends your reputation while it pulls your own index down by 0.01 a turn. The panel marks both as the Hoover line so you take them with open eyes.
Legacies

A legacy is the mark a response leaves after its immediate work is done: dearer loans for the age after a debasement, a credit cap that stays wider after lending to the crown, inflation that keeps running after leaving the gold standard. The Fiscal tab lists them under "What your choices left" with the turns each has left, or "for the age". Most clear at the age change; deposit insurance carries into the next age for a Market economy. A bank failure leaves a legacy on everyone at once.
The computer players

A computer player in a crisis takes one response per crisis, chosen by its economic system (Economic systems in the Fiscal tab). A Planned or Manorial economy builds public works; a Mercantile one supports prices, charters a company or recoins, and is the one that raises tariffs by navigation acts, in a trade collapse or when it pays trade bills; a Religious one gives relief; a Tribute economy levies tribute or debases the coin; a Palace economy debases the coin or borrows from the temple; a Market or Corporatist economy insures its deposits, or builds. A civilization whose payments pass its income declares a bank holiday first, and one at war in Modern rearms. Austerity is the player's alone. They pay the same prices and carry the same legacies you do.
The setup option

"Crises and responses" is a setup option, on by default. Off, the business cycle runs as it does without the panel: a Depression is a phase you ride out, with the legacy cushion of your old buildings and the auto-loan guard for company, and the rest of this page stays out of the game.
The temple, the grain and the debt bondage

An ancient economy had few instruments and used them hard. Debt was personal and could cost a farmer his land or his freedom; the temple was the treasury and the first bank; grain was the price everyone watched; and the coin was the ruler's to make lighter. The Antiquity responses are those levers. A Depression here opens relief, public works and the bank holiday; a debt crisis opens the cancellation of debts, the temple's loan and, for a Tribute economy, a levy on its neighbours; a price shock opens the grain dole and the debased coin.
Cancel the debts

In 594 BC Athens handed Solon the power to settle a crisis in which smallholders had mortgaged their land and then themselves. His seisachtheia, the "shaking off of burdens", cancelled the debts secured on the person, freed those enslaved for debt and forbade the practice for good. Whether he also cancelled the debts on land, and whether he cut the coinage's weight as later writers claimed, is disputed; the freeing is not.

In the game it writes off the loans your citizens and the temple treasuries hold on you, lifts your own index by 0.02 and gives each settlement 4 Happiness a turn for five turns. The price: your credit reputation falls by 20, your citizens won't lend to you again this age, and the temple treasuries charge you half as much again for 20 turns. Once per age, in a debt crisis or a Depression.
The grain dole

Rome's cura annonae began as Gaius Gracchus's subsidised grain in 123 BC and became, under Clodius in 58 BC, a free monthly ration for the citizens of the city. Emperors kept it for centuries because they didn't dare stop it: the dole was the price of a quiet capital, and a late fleet meant a riot.

In the game the dole is Antiquity's relief: 1 Gold a settlement a turn into the celebration meter, worth 4 Happiness a settlement, and a floor under this age's farm prices at nine tenths of what they were ten turns ago. It runs until the crisis ends and two turns beyond. End it early while the crisis is still on and the city remembers: 2 Happiness off each settlement for ten turns.
Debase the coin

In AD 64 Nero cut the silver in the denarius and the weight of the aureus, and the coin that had held its standard since Augustus began a decline that later emperors carried to a few percent of silver. The mint could pay the army with the same bullion stretched further; the price of everything priced in denarii followed it up.

In the game you take three turns of your income out of the temple treasuries at once, and prices rise 2 percent a turn for five turns. The legacy is the Debased mark: each loan you take for the rest of the age costs a quarter more. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a Depression or a price shock.
Public works

Pericles put Athens to work on the Acropolis from 447 BC, the Parthenon first, paid largely from the treasury of the Delian League that Athens had moved to the city. Plutarch has his critics calling it dressing the city like a vain woman, and Pericles answering that the work fed the trades of Athens.

In the game public works spends 2 Gold a settlement a turn in Antiquity (4 in Exploration, 8 in Modern) straight into your settlements' current builds, at the game's own purchase rate, through the same account a development loan uses. While it runs your own index gains 0.01 a turn, and while the world is under 0.95 each civilization building adds 0.0025 to the world's, up to 0.01 a turn in all: stimulus pulls toward Steady and stops there. It runs until the crisis ends and three turns beyond; the builds are what it leaves.
Tribute

The Persian kings ran an empire on tribute. Herodotus lists what each of Darius's satrapies owed in talents of silver, and the reliefs at Persepolis show the delegations carrying it in. A king short of silver didn't borrow; he assessed.

In the game only a Tribute economy (Despotism) can levy. Each civilization Unfriendly or worse with you that you're stronger than pays you two turns of its income at once, from what it holds, and books 10 grievances against you. Once per crisis. The legacy is the grudge: for ten turns the civilizations that paid count their trade bills to you at double, and the Fiscal tab's list shows it.
The temple lends

Temples were the first banks. The Eanna at Uruk and the temple of Shamash at Sippar lent grain and silver at interest in the third and second millennia BC; the Parthenon's treasury lent Athens the money for the Peloponnesian War and kept the account on stone. A temple loan was a loan from the city's own reserve, taken when nobody else would lend.

In the game the temple treasuries open you a loan of three turns of your income over 20 turns at the age's base rate, outside your credit cap. The legacy falls on everyone: the temple treasuries charge a quarter more, for each civilization, for the rest of the age. Once per age, in a debt crisis or a Depression.
Bank holiday

The ancient form was a moratorium: a ruler's decree that debts stood still for a season. In the game it's the same response in each age. For three turns no payment on your loans falls due or counts as missed, nobody who owes you pays either, and your escrow holds; your own index gains 0.02 once for the breathing space. Each lender's relationship with you slips by 2 and your reputation by 3. Once per age.
Confidence
A ruler who speaks to the city steadies it. In the game, 20 Influence buys 0.01 on your own index, once every five turns, in any crisis of any age. It's the cheapest response and the smallest.
Austerity

Austerity is open in each age and the same in all three: while it runs you put half of whatever you hold above your reserve into your dearest loan each turn, your reputation gains 3 once, and your own index loses 0.01 a turn. It's the right answer when your trouble is debt and the wrong one when it's demand; the panel says which your figures look like. It runs until the crisis ends.
The bankers, the bullion and the companies

Between the Medici and the Bank of England the instruments multiplied: bankers who lent to kings, kings who defaulted on them, mints that recoined, chartered companies that traded with an army, navigation acts that kept the trade at home, and fleets of silver that raised prices across Europe. The Exploration responses are those, and the crises they answer come more often: a Panic can freeze the lenders from the Banking stage, inflation runs from Public debt, and a trade collapse can follow a war or a tariff.
Suspend payments

In 1557 Philip II of Spain suspended payment on his debts, the first of four such decrees in his reign, and turned his short-term loans into long bonds by fiat. The Fuggers of Augsburg, who had financed his father's election as emperor, were never fully repaid; Genoese bankers took their place and were caught by the next suspension in turn.

In the game it's a bank holiday on the loans you owe, three turns long, with a lift of 0.02 on your own index, and the lenders remember it. Each civilization you owe loses 3 relationship and books 10 grievances, each of them refuses to lend to you again this age, and the bond market charges you half as much again for 20 turns. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a credit panic or a Depression. Two suspensions in the world within five turns start a bankruptcy cascade (see the events page).
Recoinage

By 1695 England's silver coin had been clipped to about half its lawful weight and the exchange was in disorder. The Great Recoinage of 1696 called it all in and struck it anew at full weight, at a cost to the Treasury of some two and a half million pounds, with Isaac Newton at the Mint seeing the new coin through and prosecuting the clippers.

In the game it costs two turns of your income, paid into the inflation account, and clears the inflation your own choices added (a debased coin, bullion fleets, the gold standard left). The legacy is Steadied: erosion can take at most half of what it otherwise would from your idle Gold for the rest of the age. Needs Public debt; once per age, in runaway inflation or a price shock.
Charter a company

Elizabeth I chartered the East India Company on the last day of 1600, with a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape; the Dutch VOC followed in 1602 as the first company to sell shares to the public. Both paid dividends to their shareholders for two centuries, and both ended up ruling the places they had been chartered to trade with.

In the game, for 20 turns your credit cap gains two turns of income and your trade bills fall by a fifth. The company can't be closed: for the rest of the age a fifth of your route income goes to its shareholders, your citizens. Needs the Chartered companies stage and a trade route; once per age, in a trade collapse, a Depression or a debt crisis.
Navigation acts

England's Navigation Act of 1651 and its successors kept colonial trade in English ships and routed it through English ports: mercantilism as law. They fed three wars with the Dutch, who had carried that trade, and were repealed only in 1849.

In the game it sets your tariff to High for ten turns without the relationship cost a High tariff usually carries, and the civilizations you import from can't answer it in kind while it stands, since the acts are law. The legacy is the Hoover line's: for the rest of the age you count double toward a trade war. Needs the Tariffs stage; once per age, in a trade collapse, a price shock or a Depression.
Bullion fleets

From the 1540s the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas crossed the Atlantic in convoys, and Spain spent it. Prices in Spain and then across Europe rose for a century, the "price revolution"; how much of that was the silver and how much population growth is still argued, but the crown's income rose with the fleets and its wars rose faster.

In the game a fleet lands three turns of your income at once, and prices rise 3 percent a turn for five turns. The legacies: your own inflation runs 0.25 percent a turn faster for ten turns, and for 20 turns the pirates are out, so a trade collapse comes at half the loss of routes it otherwise takes. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a Depression or a credit panic.
Lend to the crown

The Medici bank lent to popes and kings and lived on it; the Fuggers lent Charles V the money that bought the imperial election of 1519 and took the Habsburg silver mines as security. A banker that deep in a crown's affairs couldn't let it fail without failing too.

In the game it needs a civilization Friendly with you that holds Gold. Your credit cap gains four turns of income for the rest of the age, as its lenders extend themselves on your account. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a credit panic or a Depression.
Public works

Thomas Gresham built London's Exchange in 1565 at his own expense and Elizabeth I named it Royal in 1571; the canal age that began with the Bridgewater in 1761 was dug on borrowed money and paid for itself in coal. In the game public works in Exploration spends 4 Gold a settlement a turn into your builds, with the same 0.01 a turn on your own index and the same world share under 0.95 as in Antiquity. It runs until the crisis ends and three turns beyond.
Relief

The English Poor Laws of 1601 made each parish responsible for its own poor and taxed it to pay for them. In the game relief is 1 Gold a settlement a turn into the celebration meter, worth 4 Happiness a settlement, until the crisis ends and two turns beyond; Emigration and Partisans read it as Happiness. Ending it early while the crisis is on costs 2 Happiness a settlement for ten turns.
Bank holiday

Three turns with no payment due or missed on your loans and none owed to you; 0.02 on your own index once; 2 relationship with each lender and 3 reputation. Once per age, in each of the three. Suspending payments is the harder version, above.
Confidence
20 Influence for 0.01 on your own index, once every five turns, in any crisis.
Austerity
Half of what you hold above your reserve into your dearest loan each turn, 3 reputation once, and 0.01 a turn off your own index while it runs. The Hoover line in any age.
The New Deal

The Great Depression began with the crash of October 1929 and ran, in the United States, to the war. Between 1929 and 1933 output fell by about a third, a quarter of the workforce was out of work, and some nine thousand banks failed. Herbert Hoover's administration raised tariffs, balanced budgets and waited; Franklin Roosevelt's first hundred days, from March 1933, tried most of what is on this page at once. The Modern responses are the New Deal, with the Hoover line kept on the panel so you can see what it cost.
Bank holiday

Roosevelt closed the country's banks on 6 March 1933, two days after his inauguration, and the Emergency Banking Act of 9 March let the sound ones reopen under licence. Deposits flowed back in the week after, which is the whole point of a holiday: it stops the run long enough for confidence to return.

In the game, for three turns no payment on your loans falls due or counts as missed and nobody who owes you pays; your escrow holds and your own index gains 0.02 once. Each lender's relationship with you slips by 2 and your reputation by 3. Once per age.
Deposit insurance

The Banking Act of June 1933, Glass-Steagall, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and parted commercial banking from securities. Insured deposits ended the bank run as an American institution: with the government standing behind the account there was no longer a reason to be first in the queue.

In the game it costs two turns of your income, paid into the bond market as the fund, and lasts the age (a Market economy carries it into the next). While it stands a Panic hits your own index half as hard and the freeze on lenders doesn't apply to you, the bond market's spread never rises above 1.0 for you, and a bank run can't happen to you; the price is a credit cap whose depth term is cut by a quarter, since insured banks lend less. Needs the Banking stage; once in the game, in a credit panic, a Depression or a debt crisis.
Off the gold standard

In April 1933 the United States stopped paying out gold and called in the gold coin, and in January 1934 the dollar was fixed again at 35 dollars an ounce, down from 20.67: a devaluation of 41 percent. Britain had left gold in September 1931. The countries that left first recovered first; the ones that stayed on it, France among them, stayed down longest.

In the game the loans you owe the bond market, the temple treasuries and your citizens lose a tenth of what's outstanding, prices rise 3 percent a turn for five turns, your inflation runs 0.5 percent a turn faster for those five turns and then 0.25 percent faster for the rest of the age, and your own index gains 0.01 a turn for five turns. Each civilization you owe loses 3 relationship and books 10 grievances, and your reputation falls by 10. A Planned economy has no money to float. Needs Public debt; once per age, in a Depression, a debt crisis or a credit panic. Ten turns off gold opens a runaway-inflation crisis; a recoinage answers it.
Public works

The Civilian Conservation Corps put young men to work in the forests from 1933; the Tennessee Valley Authority dammed a river system; the Works Progress Administration of 1935 employed more than eight million people over its life building roads, schools, airports and bridges, and paid writers and painters too. Deficit spending as a cure for a slump had its theory in Keynes's General Theory of 1936, but the works came first.

In the game public works in Modern spends 8 Gold a settlement a turn into your settlements' current builds through the progress account, with 0.01 a turn on your own index and, while the world is under 0.95, 0.0025 on the world's for each civilization building, up to 0.01 a turn in all. It runs until the crisis ends and three turns beyond; the builds stay.
Relief

The Federal Emergency Relief Administration of 1933 sent money to the states for direct relief, Britain's dole had carried its unemployed since 1911, and the Social Security Act of 1935 made the relief of old age permanent. In the game relief is 1 Gold a settlement a turn into the celebration meter, 4 Happiness a settlement, until the crisis ends and two turns beyond; the Emigration and Partisans mods read it as Happiness. End it early while the crisis is on and each settlement loses 2 Happiness a turn for ten turns.
Price supports

The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to grow less so that prices would rise, and the National Recovery Administration's codes set prices and wages across industry until the Supreme Court struck the NRA down in 1935. Farm prices did recover; whether the codes helped or held recovery back is still argued.

In the game it puts a floor under this age's farm (Bonus) resource prices at nine tenths of what they were ten turns ago, for everyone, and you pay for it: half your income a turn into the cycle account while it runs. It runs until the crisis ends. The price abroad is dearer imports: while it runs, each civilization that imports from you loses 1 relationship every five turns, and the Fiscal tab keeps the mark for ten turns after. Once per crisis, in a price shock, a Depression or a trade collapse.
Rearmament

In the game, for ten turns your own index gains 0.005 a turn, the army costs you 1 Gold a settlement a turn, and a computer player's army budget runs at one and a half times its usual weight. The neighbours notice: the turn you take it, every civilization whose capital is within 20 plots of yours loses 1 relationship with you. That notice is the legacy, on the list for 20 turns. Once per age, in a Depression, a trade collapse or a credit panic.
Confidence

Roosevelt's first fireside chat, on 12 March 1933, explained the bank holiday to the country in plain words, and the banks reopened the next morning to queues of depositors putting money back. In the game, 20 Influence buys 0.01 on your own index, once every five turns, in any crisis.
The Hoover trap

The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of June 1930 raised duties on some twenty thousand goods over the objection of a thousand economists; America's partners answered in kind, and world trade fell by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934. Andrew Mellon, Hoover's Treasury Secretary, is remembered for the advice to "liquidate labor, liquidate stocks, liquidate the farmers"; the words come from Hoover's memoirs, but the policy of balanced budgets in a slump was Hoover's own, and when Roosevelt tried it himself in 1937 the recovery stalled for a year.

In the game both are on the panel, marked. A High tariff in a Depression is answered in kind by the computer players you bill, each route that ends weighs 0.005 on the index, and once three civilizations hold High while the world is under 0.80 the trade war takes 0.005 more a turn from everyone. Austerity repays debt with half your surplus each turn and gains you 3 reputation, and takes 0.01 a turn from your own index while it runs. The panel tells you whether your figures look like a debt problem or a demand problem before you choose.
Read from the state, not rolled

The events on this page are read, not rolled: each one is a reading the mod takes each turn from the ledger, the cycle and the map, and each has a history behind it. They make a crisis worse, or mark its end.
A bank run

The Bank of United States in New York failed in December 1930 with four hundred thousand depositors, the largest bank failure in the country's history to that day, and the runs spread from bank to bank through 1931 and 1932. A bank fails when enough of what it lent out goes bad at once and its depositors notice.

In the game a civilization in a Depression with two or more borrowers in default to it takes a run: its own index loses 0.02 once and it lends to nobody for five turns. Once per Depression. Deposit insurance stops it.
Bank failures

Some nine thousand American banks failed between 1930 and 1933, and with them the deposits of their customers and the lending of the rest, which is how a run becomes a depression. In the game, when the loans in default pass a fifth of all the world's loans while the world is in a Depression, the bond market closes for five turns to each civilization without deposit insurance, and each credit cap in the world loses two turns of income for the rest of the age. Once per age.
The Dust Bowl

Drought on the ploughed-up plains from 1930 lifted the topsoil into storms that reached the Atlantic, and a farm economy already in a depression lost its land and its people to the roads. In the game a disaster on the land of a civilization in Depression (a flood, a storm, an eruption) weighs twice on its index: the disaster's usual weight, and the Dust Bowl's again.
The Bonus Army

In the summer of 1932 some forty thousand people, veterans of the Great War and their families, camped in Washington to ask for the bonus they'd been promised for 1945, and in July the army cleared them out with cavalry, tanks and tear gas. A government that leaves its people to a depression hears from them. In the game a civilization five turns into a Depression with neither relief nor public works running loses 0.01 a turn on its own index until it starts one.
A bubble, and its burst

Tulips in 1637, the South Sea Company in 1720, stocks bought on margin in 1929: a boom in which credit grows faster than the thing it's buying, until the turn. In the game, when the world has read "credit growing fast" five turns running with the index above 1.05, the notice says a bubble is on. If the index then falls under 0.95 within fifteen turns, it bursts: a credit panic opens for each civilization holding loans, in the ages that have one. A bubble that deflates slowly instead is forgotten.
A bankruptcy cascade

When Philip II suspended payment, the bankers who had lent to him couldn't pay the ones who had lent to them, and the stoppage ran through Antwerp and Augsburg. In the game two suspensions of payments in the world within five turns close the bond market to each civilization without deposit insurance for five turns.
Recovery

A crisis ends the turn its condition stops holding. The notice names what ended it, the responses you took during it or the world recovering on its own, and the chronicle on the Treasury tab keeps the line. The responses that ran "until the crisis ends" wind down over their last few turns, and the legacies stay for as long as each says on the Fiscal tab.
Crises: own answers
Programme
Every government has its own answers

Besides the responses every civilization can take, some governments and ideologies have answers only they can reach for. A Classical Republic can borrow from its citizens as a public duty, a Plutocracy can charter its merchants or turn its debts into shares, a Democracy can run New Deal programmes or regulate its banks, and a Fascist state can export its crisis into a war. They show on the World tab's Crisis section under "Your government's own answers" while a crisis runs.
Each answer costs Influence to take, because each one spends political capital. Your Influence has to cover the price before you can take it, and the price shows on the card.
Measures, Programmes and Gambles

A Measure is quick relief: cheap, small and short, with its price landing within a few turns. A Programme is a structural fix: it costs Influence every turn and an administration charge in Gold, your own loans cost a quarter more while it runs, and it has to run at least five turns, but it works on the crisis turn after turn. A Gamble is a fast fix with a catch written on the card: it pays off if things go your way and turns on you if they don't.

No tier is best everywhere. Measures suit a short, shallow crisis or a thin Influence purse; Programmes suit a deep, long one with Influence to spend; Gambles suit a civilization that can't afford a Programme and can meet the Gamble's condition.
How a Programme ends

A Programme is Running from the turn you take it, and has its minimum run done once it has run five turns with every payment made. When the crisis is over and the five turns are done, it's judged on its own goal, shown on the card: the citizens' loan repaid on schedule, the works grants paid in full, your loan payments brought down, and so on. Until then the outcome isn't final.

Meet the goal and it leaves a lasting institution, listed on the Fiscal tab. Miss it and you get an institution with costs and no benefit. End it early, or fail a payment, and it leaves its own mark. A Programme judged while your economy is still under 0.80 counts as a missed goal at best. One institution a crisis, and one Programme at a time.
How your crises shape you

Every institution you earn makes that path a step cheaper next time and your other paths a step dearer, 5% a step and never more than 15% either way. Earning a different path later moves the old one back. Over a game, a civilization that keeps answering crises the same way finds that way easier, and its history shows on the Fiscal tab under "How your crises have shaped you".
A Classical Republic: the citizens' republic

Athens asked its richest citizens to pay for warships and festivals as a public duty, the liturgy. Land reform, the old demand of land for the landless, set the poor against the great families, as the Gracchi found in Rome.

In the game, Liturgies borrows from your citizens at no interest against a fall in Public support while the loan stands; Land reform buys support with Gold and smaller citizens' loans; The assembly speaks lifts confidence now and turns on you if the economy hasn't recovered five turns later. The game leaves out who paid and who gained: it models the money and the mood, not the classes.
A Plutocracy: the company state

The great merchant companies borrowed against their charters to build ships and docks. In 1711 a trading company took over a nation's debts in exchange for its shares, and the bubble that followed burst. In 1694 a state raised a million by selling lottery tickets that paid interest.

In the game, Merchant charter borrows to put production into your builds for each trade route you run; Debt into shares writes off part of your bond debt in exchange for a claim on your income; Lottery loan is cheap money repaid fast. The game leaves out the shareholders themselves and the scandal: it keeps the claim on your income and the risk of the burst.
A Democracy: public investment and financial reform

The New Deal of 1933 to 1939 put the unemployed to work on public works and built Social Security; it was contested in its day and never complete, and historians still argue over how much it ended the Depression. Glass-Steagall separated banks that take deposits from banks that speculate. Lend-Lease sent arms and food on credit to friends at war.

In the game, New Deal programmes run Public works and Relief at half the Gold, with the bond market paying the rest; Bank regulation makes your loans cheaper while cutting your credit limit, and earned it softens a Panic; Lend-lease doubles the goodwill of aid to civilizations at war, and you can send it while you stay at peace. The game leaves out the politics of passing them: their price in Influence stands in for it.
A Fascist state: the war economy

More than one regime of the 1930s turned a crisis at home into a closed economy and a war abroad, paid for in part with paper a central bank quietly backed. The game takes the economic mechanism and leaves the regimes' crimes to history; nothing on these cards measures what they cost the people who lived and died under them.

In the game, Diversionary war commits you to fighting within five turns: while at war your military builds get production and the bond market pays your army's upkeep, which you owe later; Self-sufficiency closes your trade behind High tariffs; Off-book bills give Gold now that only conquest pays down. They work fast, and they leave you dependent on expansion: a war economy at peace starts to slide.
Hardship and Partisans

With the Partisans mod on, a deep Depression is felt in the countryside. While your economy is under 0.80, each settlement counts up to 6 less Happiness toward a partisan rising, more the deeper it goes. Relief or New Deal programmes halve it; Austerity adds to it. Your settlements' own Happiness doesn't change: only the count toward a rising does, and the Crisis section and the City Details panel show it.
